evidence_quotes.page: PMC4980313 - The Role of the state
evidence_quotes.quote: As the correlation between the two variables, state interventions, and existence of proportional equality reveals (phi = −0.478, P = 0.000), the involvement of the state can explain the institutional outcome to a significant degree.

We, therefore, base our analysis of the success of the water management regimes on social indicators developed in cooperation with communities. These include (1) satisfaction with the rules, (2) satisfaction with the work of the water point committee (committee), (3) general level of satisfaction expressed concerning cooperation in the community, and (4) the general satisfaction with the water management in the community.

While this could have to do with higher reliability and better “performance” of boreholes that are managed under proportional equality, there is no correlation between the sharing rule and the susceptibility of the technological infrastructure and thus water access or supply (phi = −0.01, non-significant). Combined with our ethnographic observations, this indicates that success is mostly judged socially.

printed_headline_estimate: State involvement vs. adoption of proportional payment rule: phi = -0.478, P = 0.000 (N <= 56 communities, 'The Role of the state'); Proportional vs. numerical payment rule on perceived social satisfaction (Table 1, N < 60 communities): institutional rules rbc = 0.559 (P = 0.000), committee work rbc = 0.427 (P = 0.017), community cooperation rbc = 0.406 (P = 0.006), general satisfaction with water management rbc = 0.389 (P = 0.003); Solar/diesel technology vs. payment rule: phi = 0.155, P = 0.244; Parenthetical check of sharing rule vs. borehole infrastructure susceptibility/water access or supply: phi = -0.01, non-significant (no exact P, SE/CI, N, or coding polarity printed, 'Levels of success'); Household water-share and wealth Gini trajectories (Fig. 1, 80 households) are outputs of a deterministic 100-month simulation model.
publication_year_note: Retrieved PMC OA XML (PMC4980313) omits the journal front-matter metadata block; 2016 is indicated by the DOI (10.1007/s13280-016-0766-9) and in-text citations up to 2016 (Schnegg and Bollig 2016), so online-first vs. print volume/issue dates cannot be distinguished from the XML body text alone.
rationale: The study conducts comparative quantitative tests across up to 56-60 pastoralist communities in northwestern Namibia alongside a 100-month simulation model calibrated to 80 households, but none of its fully reported inferential tests evaluate a Criterion 4 physical/economic water service access outcome. Specifically: (1) phi = -0.478 (P = 0.000) tests state extension involvement on institutional rule choice (whether a community adopts a proportional per-livestock vs. flat numerical per-household fee rule), and phi = 0.155 (P = 0.244) tests solar/diesel pump technology on fee rule choice, both failing Criterion 4; (2) Table 1 (rbc = 0.559, P = 0.000; rbc = 0.427, P = 0.017; rbc = 0.406, P = 0.006; rbc = 0.389, P = 0.003) tests proportional vs. flat water tariff rules on four subjective social satisfaction ratings (rules, committee work, community cooperation, and general water management), which the authors explicitly characterize as social perception indicators rather than physical water supply/access; and (3) the distributional analysis of household water consumption shares and livestock wealth inequality under flat fees (Fig. 1) is a deterministic simulation model rather than an empirical inferential test. A single parenthetical remark in 'Levels of success' notes no correlation between the sharing/payment rule and 'the susceptibility of the technological infrastructure and thus water access or supply (phi = -0.01, non-significant)', which touches a Criterion 2 tariff rule and Criterion 4 borehole reliability/supply construct, but omits any numerical P-value, SE/CI/test statistic, sample size N, and variable operationalization or binary coding polarity (notably, unstated coding polarity in the same dataset yielded a negative sign phi = -0.478 for positive state support), leaving no directionally interpretable or p-value-combinable SWiM effect estimate.
